front_blocks.md: What is the purpose of paper chromatography?

back_blocks.md: Paper chromatography is used to **separate** mixtures of soluble coloured substances and to **identify** the components by comparing them with known reference samples.

cards.front_md: What is the purpose of paper chromatography?
cards.back_md: Paper chromatography is used to **separate** mixtures of soluble coloured substances and to **identify** the components by comparing them with known reference samples.

front_blocks.md: *R*<sub>f</sub> = distance moved by **..........** divided by distance moved by **..........** .

back_blocks.md: *R*<sub>f</sub> = distance moved by **substance** divided by distance moved by **solvent**.

front_blocks.md: Why must the pencil line on chromatography paper be drawn above the level of the solvent?

back_blocks.md: The pencil line must be **above the solvent level** so that the sample spots are not washed directly into the solvent, which would prevent them from separating on the paper.

cards.front_md: Why must the pencil line on chromatography paper be drawn above the level of the solvent?
cards.back_md: The pencil line must be **above the solvent level** so that the sample spots are not washed directly into the solvent, which would prevent them from separating on the paper.

front_blocks.md: A pure substance will produce more than one spot on a chromatogram.

back_blocks.md: A pure substance produces only one spot on a chromatogram. More than one spot indicates a mixture or an impure substance.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

A pure substance will produce more than one spot on a chromatogram.
cards.back_md:
**False.**

A pure substance produces only one spot on a chromatogram. More than one spot indicates a mixture or an impure substance.

front_blocks.md: How do you identify whether an unknown substance on a chromatogram matches a known reference substance?

back_blocks.md: If the spot from the unknown substance travels the **same distance** as a spot from the known reference substance (they are at the same horizontal level), the two substances are the same.

cards.front_md: How do you identify whether an unknown substance on a chromatogram matches a known reference substance?
cards.back_md: If the spot from the unknown substance travels the **same distance** as a spot from the known reference substance (they are at the same horizontal level), the two substances are the same.

front_blocks.md: A substance that is more **..........** in the solvent will travel further up the chromatography paper.

back_blocks.md: A substance that is more **soluble** in the solvent will travel further up the chromatography paper.

cards.front_md: A substance that is more **..........** in the solvent will travel further up the chromatography paper.
cards.back_md: A substance that is more **soluble** in the solvent will travel further up the chromatography paper.

front_blocks.md: Why is pencil used to draw the baseline on chromatography paper rather than ink?

back_blocks.md: Pencil is used because ink would **dissolve** in the solvent and run up the paper along with the samples, interfering with the results. Pencil marks do not dissolve.

cards.front_md: Why is pencil used to draw the baseline on chromatography paper rather than ink?

front_blocks.md: Which separation technique is used to separate an undissolved solid from a liquid?

back_blocks.md: **Filtration** is used to separate an undissolved solid from a liquid. The solid remains as a residue in the filter paper while the liquid passes through as the filtrate.

cards.front_md: Which separation technique is used to separate an undissolved solid from a liquid?
cards.back_md: **Filtration** is used to separate an undissolved solid from a liquid. The solid remains as a residue in the filter paper while the liquid passes through as the filtrate.

front_blocks.md: Simple distillation separates a dissolved solid from its **..........** , whereas fractional distillation separates two **..........** liquids.

back_blocks.md: Simple distillation separates a dissolved solid from its **solvent**, whereas fractional distillation separates two **miscible** liquids.

cards.front_md: Simple distillation separates a dissolved solid from its **..........** , whereas fractional distillation separates two **..........** liquids.
cards.back_md: Simple distillation separates a dissolved solid from its **solvent**, whereas fractional distillation separates two **miscible** liquids.

front_blocks.md: How does crystallisation separate a dissolved solid from a solution?

back_blocks.md: Crystallisation separates a dissolved solid from a solution by heating the solution to concentrate it, then allowing it to cool slowly so that **crystals form** as the solubility of the solid decreases. The crystals are then collected by **filtration**.

cards.front_md: How does crystallisation separate a dissolved solid from a solution?
cards.back_md: Crystallisation separates a dissolved solid from a solution by heating the solution to concentrate it, then allowing it to cool slowly so that **crystals form** as the solubility of the solid decreases. The crystals are then collected by **filtration**.

front_blocks.md: A pure substance melts over a range of temperatures, while an impure substance melts at a single sharp temperature.

back_blocks.md: A pure substance has a single, sharp melting point. An impure substance (a mixture) melts over a range of temperatures because it contains different components.

cards.front_md:
**True or False?**

A pure substance melts over a range of temperatures, while an impure substance melts at a single sharp temperature.
cards.back_md:
**False.**

A pure substance has a single, sharp melting point. An impure substance (a mixture) melts over a range of temperatures because it contains different components.

front_blocks.md: How do impurities affect the melting point and boiling point of a substance?

back_blocks.md: Impurities **lower the melting point** and **raise the boiling point** of a substance compared to the pure substance. The more impure the sample, the greater the effect on these values.

cards.front_md: How do impurities affect the melting point and boiling point of a substance?
cards.back_md: Impurities **lower the melting point** and **raise the boiling point** of a substance compared to the pure substance. The more impure the sample, the greater the effect on these values.

front_blocks.md: In fractional distillation of ethanol and water, **..........** distils out first because it has a lower **..........** point of 78 °C.

back_blocks.md: In fractional distillation of ethanol and water, **ethanol** distils out first because it has a lower **boiling** point of 78 °C.

cards.front_md: In fractional distillation of ethanol and water, **..........** distils out first because it has a lower **..........** point of 78 °C.
cards.back_md: In fractional distillation of ethanol and water, **ethanol** distils out first because it has a lower **boiling** point of 78 °C.

front_blocks.md: Why is fractional distillation used rather than simple distillation to separate ethanol from water?

back_blocks.md: Fractional distillation is used because ethanol and water have boiling points that are relatively close together (78 °C and 100 °C). Fractional distillation achieves a **higher degree of purity** when separating liquids with similar boiling points.
